rq: Is air connectivity clean connectivity? Trade and openness have ambiguous effects on the environment because scale, composition and technique effects pull in different directions (Grossman and Krueger 1993; Antweiler, Copeland and Taylor 2001; Managi, Hibiki and Tsurumi 2009). This paper asks a narrower question: when a country becomes more central in the global air network, does the pollution and carbon intensity of its economy fall, and if so through which of the three channels?

Air connectivity is measured with the Global Air Connectivity Index (GACI), a within-year standardised composite of degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector and regional-importance centrality of each airport, aggregated to the country by seat-weighted mean. Because aviation itself emits under 3% of national CO2 and a negligible share of SO2, any effect on national intensities must run through the economy, not through aircraft.

Hypotheses. H1 (clean connectivity): higher air connectivity lowers SO2, NOx and CO2 per unit of GDP and raises the renewable share. H2 (technique, not composition): the reduction occurs within fuels, as lower emissions per unit of fuel burned, and is not explained by shifts in industrial structure. H3 (where): the effect is concentrated in goods-producing economies that have plants and power stations to retrofit, not in service economies.

Design. Country-year panel, 149 countries, 1996–2019 (unified sample). ln y = b ln GACI + ln pop + ln GDP pc + (ln GDP pc)^2 + country FE + year FE, standard errors clustered by country. Feyrer-type air market access instruments GACI in the IV tables. The GACI coefficient is an elasticity; one within-country standard deviation of ln GACI is 0.07, so a one-SD move changes an outcome by about 7% of the coefficient.
T1: Air connectivity is associated with cleaner production per unit of GDP: a 1% higher GACI lowers SO2 intensity by about 0.9% and NOx intensity by 0.3%, raises the renewable share by 8 points per log unit, and lowers CO2 and energy intensity by about 0.3%. The fuel mix (CO2 per unit of energy) does not move. One within-country SD of connectivity translates into 7% lower SO2 intensity and 2 to 3% lower carbon and energy intensity. The income terms trace the usual inverted-U Kuznets curve.
T2: The SO2 reduction is a technique effect in the Antweiler–Copeland–Taylor sense: coal combustion does not fall (if anything it rises), yet SO2 emitted per unit of coal and oil burned falls by roughly 1% per 1% of GACI. Because a fuel's emission factor depends only on its sulphur content and on end-of-pipe desulphurisation, this isolates abatement technology and fuel standards. Process SO2 from smelters and refineries, whose location is fixed by geology, does not respond, which serves as a placebo.
T3: Adding industrial composition (manufacturing, services, agriculture shares), openness (trade, FDI) and urbanisation barely moves the GACI coefficient; all observable channels together account for under 10% of it. The composition effect, the channel emphasised in the pollution-haven literature, is not what drives the result. Combined with Table 2 this leaves technique as the operative channel.
T4: The clean-connectivity effect lives in goods-producing economies: in countries with above-median merchandise trade in 1996 the GACI coefficients on NOx, renewables and CO2 intensity are large and significant, while in service economies they are zero or positive. By income, the SO2 effect is concentrated in the low-income tercile. Both patterns fit a story of technology and standards reaching industrial economies that still have abatement to install, and do not fit a tourism-pressure story.
T5: Instrumenting GACI with Feyrer-type air market access (first-stage F about 12) confirms the sign for every outcome and yields coefficients several times larger than OLS, as is typical when the regressor is a noisy within-year relative measure. The heritage-times-tourism instrument has no first-stage power in this sample and is used only in the over-identified model; the Sargan test does not reject for SO2, renewables and CO2 intensity but rejects for NOx. We treat the IV estimates as supporting evidence on direction, not as the preferred magnitudes.
A1a: The SO2 result survives adding capital-labour ratio and trade openness (Managi et al. controls) and a geographic sea-connectivity control, and is strongest in 1996–2009. It weakens and loses significance when the comparison is restricted within region-years or within income-group-years, when liner shipping connectivity (2006–) is added, and in 2010–2019. GACI is a relative, within-year index, so these stricter designs remove much of its variation; we report them as the boundary of what the country panel can identify.
A1b: The CO2-intensity result is weaker and less stable than the SO2 result: it is robust to Managi-style controls and to the sea-connectivity control, becomes stronger with LSCI in the 2006+ window and in 2010–2019, but is zero under region-by-year or income-group-by-year effects. CO2 is the expected weak outcome of the mechanism: desulphurisation does not reduce CO2, and the only CO2 channel we find is energy efficiency (Table 1).
A2: Results are not an artefact of the aggregation rule. The seat-weighted mean of airport GACI (used throughout) and its level give the same picture; the unweighted mean across all airports is smaller and insignificant, because it dilutes hub airports with many small ones. Connectivity of the airports that carry traffic is what matters.
